slides.say: Given: p is smaller than q, which is smaller than zero, which is smaller than r, which is smaller than s. Which of the following is necessarily true?

So we know the order of four numbers. And look at the answers, every one of them uses absolute value. And what's absolute value? Distance from zero. So the question is really, who is further from zero? [short pause] Two ways, the number line, and then plugging in numbers.
[short pause] Our first method. Let's put them on the number line. p and q are negative, and p is further to the left. r and s are positive, and s is further to the right.
There are two things we can promise. s is always further from zero than r, both on the right. And p is always further from zero than q, both on the left. We don't know by how much, but always.

But a negative against a positive? The negatives could be negative one and negative three, and the positives a thousand and seven thousand. Or the other way around. We only know the order, not the numbers.
So number one compares r and p, a positive and a negative. Not necessarily, out. Number three, p and s, different sides again, out. Number four, q and s, different sides, out.

Three are out, so in the exam you'd circle number two and move on. Here, let's see why it's right. q and p are both negative, and p is further from zero. So the absolute value of q is smaller than the absolute value of p. Number two is our answer.

[pause] Our second method, plugging in numbers. The givens only fix the order, not the sizes. So the trick is to try two extreme pictures. First, the negatives far from zero and the positives close to it. p is negative fifty, q negative forty, r one and s three. They're in order, so they obey the given.

Number one, one smaller than fifty? Yes, it stays. Number two, forty smaller than fifty? Yes, it stays. Number three, fifty smaller than three? No, out. Number four, forty smaller than three? No, out.
at: fifty? Yes, it stays. Number three

slides.say: Now the opposite picture, the negatives close to zero and the positives far. p is negative three, q negative one, r forty and s fifty.
Number one, forty smaller than three? No, out. Number two, one smaller than three? Yes, and it worked in the first picture too. So number two survives both pictures. Number two.

So when the letters sit on both sides of zero, try one picture with the negatives far away, and one with the positives far away. Same side, you can compare. Different sides, you can't. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
